title: Stop Doing This When Parking On A Hill
hook: Stop turning your wheels straight when you park on a slope.

script.narration: Stop turning your wheels straight when you park on a slope. Most drivers park incorrectly every single day, leaving their vehicle completely vulnerable to rolling away if a brake ever fails. Today, you are going to learn the exact steering wheel and parking brake routine that keeps your car totally secure on any incline, whether there is a curb or not. By the end of this quick guide, you will never have to second-guess how you leave your car parked again. Let us break down the physics of gravity and the simple steps to keep your vehicle locked in place safely.
script.visual_search: car parked on a steep street exterior

script.narration: Think about what actually holds your car in place when you park. It is not a massive anchor or a thick steel cable. Inside your automatic transmission is a tiny metal pin called a parking pawl, and it is roughly the size of your finger. That small piece of metal is the only thing stopping your entire vehicle from rolling down the street when you park on a slope. If that pin slips or snaps under the weight of the car, gravity takes over instantly. Suddenly, a two-ton vehicle turns into a runaway boulder. Relying entirely on the 'Park' gear on a hill is a huge gamble that many drivers take every single day without realizing the risk. Even if your brakes feel totally solid, leaning the weight of the car against that single internal part creates massive wear over time. But there is a very simple physical trick using your front wheels that completely neutralizes this danger before you even turn off the engine.
script.visual_search: car sliding down a hill danger

script.narration: When parking uphill alongside a curb, your steering wheel needs a very specific turn. You want to crank your front wheels sharply away from the curb, out toward the middle of the street. Here is why this simple habit saves cars. If your parking brake ever gives out, your car will start to roll backward. As it moves, the back edge of your front tire will gently hit the curb and lock right against it. That concrete edge acts as a natural wheel chock, stopping the car from rolling all the way down the hill into traffic. It is a tiny adjustment that completely changes your safety. If you are learning something, subscribe, it helps a lot. But what happens if you pull up to that exact same uphill slope, and there is no curb at all to catch your tires?
script.visual_search: driver turning steering wheel close up

script.narration: What happens when you park uphill and there is no curb in sight? This is where many drivers accidentally put themselves and others in danger. Without a concrete barrier to catch your tires, the direction of your wheels becomes your only safety net. For this scenario, you want to turn your front tires sharply toward the edge of the road, pointing them right toward the shoulder or dirt. Think of it this way: if your brakes ever give out, gravity is going to pull the car backward. By angling your wheels right, the car will safely veer off the asphalt and onto the grass or dirt, instead of rolling backward into active traffic lanes. It is a simple adjustment that completely changes where a runaway car ends up. But what if you are facing the exact opposite direction on a steep slope with no curb? That requires a totally different trick.
script.visual_search: car parked on country road side view

script.narration: Now let us look at what happens when you park facing downhill. Gravity is naturally pulling your car forward, so your main goal is to keep it from rolling away if your parking brake ever slips. Whether you have a concrete curb right next to you or just the dirt shoulder of the road, your strategy here is very specific. You want to turn your steering wheel all the way toward the edge of the road, pointing your front tires right in toward the curb or side. If your brakes somehow fail, your vehicle will gently roll forward and the front tires will catch against the curb or shoulder, acting like a natural wooden block. It stops the car from gaining speed and becoming a runaway hazard. But what happens if you forget this step and leave your wheels pointed straight ahead? That tiny mistake can turn a simple grocery run into an expensive towing nightmare. Up next, we reveal the absolute final step most drivers forget to do before walking away.
script.visual_search: car parked facing down a steep hill

script.narration: The most important part of this entire routine, which saves your transmission from permanent damage, is engaging your parking brake before you shift your automatic car into Park and take your foot off the foot brake. This simple habit ensures the heavy weight of the vehicle rests securely on the brake pads rather than straining the delicate internal transmission gears. Imagine the entire weight of your car hanging on a metal pin the size of your pinky finger every time you park on a slope without doing this. By letting the parking brake take the load first, you prevent that terrible clunk sound and the stuck gear shifter the next time you try to drive away. What type of hill gives you the most anxiety when parking? Let us know in the comments below. But before you drive off, there is one more crucial mistake drivers make when leaving their car that can lead to a runaway vehicle.

To quickly recap what we covered today: always turn your front wheels the correct way relative to the curb so your car has a physical block if it rolls, and remember to engage your emergency parking brake firmly before shifting your transmission into park. This simple two-step routine takes just a few seconds, but it completely removes the risk of your vehicle slipping away while you are away from it. Let us know in the comments: have you ever seen a car roll down a hill because the driver forgot this trick? Drop your thoughts below. If you want to master more everyday driving skills in under a minute, make sure to watch the next video on our channel right now.
